Introduction: Science, Math, and... Tea?

Alright, let’s get ourselves settled! Today, we are going to do things a little differently. Instead of just staring at the board, we are going to run a live experiment. I have brought in some hot water, cups, and a selection of teas—lemon, Japanese green tea, decaf, you name it. We are going to use this strictly for scientific purposes (though you are welcome to drink it once it cools down to a safe level).

Your job today is to act as the data acquisition system. I am going to pour hot water into your cups, and I want you to measure the temperature as a function of time. You don’t have to stare at the thermometer constantly; just take a reading every few minutes. We will compile all this data to see how it connects to the math we are about to discuss.

While we wait for the water to cool, let’s talk about differential equations. Over the past few lectures, we reviewed calculus—taking derivatives, evaluating integrals, and discussing what those operations physically mean. Today, we take it one step further.

Some of you might have taken a differential equations course already, and some haven’t. I assure you, it is not going to matter in the least! In a standard math class, they often teach you the mechanics of solving these equations without necessarily showing you how they apply to real, everyday situations—like a cooling cup of tea. We are going to prioritize the physical intuition today.

A Quick Review: Algebraic Equations

Before we dive into the new stuff, let’s ground ourselves by looking at the types of equations you are already very used to seeing: algebraic equations.

Imagine you are a real estate agent, a farmer, or perhaps the ruler of a kingdom, and you need to divide up land fairly. You are given a puzzle: What width, w, do you need to make a square plot of land that has the exact same area as a specific combination of other plots? Let’s say the other plots are a rectangular piece of land that is 2 meters wide by w meters long, plus a leftover square patch that is exactly 3 square meters.

We can visualize this geometric problem like so:

To solve this, we translate the geometry into algebra. The area of the large square is w \times w = w^2. The area of the rectangle is 2 \times w = 2w. The final piece is just 3. Setting them equal gives us our algebraic equation: \begin{equation} w^2 = 2w + 3 \tag{1} \end{equation} To solve for w, we move everything to one side to form a standard quadratic equation: \begin{equation} w^2 - 2w - 3 = 0 \tag{2} \end{equation} If you are feeling fancy, you can factor this polynomial. We need two numbers that multiply to -3 and add to -2. Those numbers are -3 and +1: \begin{equation} (w + 1)(w - 3) = 0 \tag{3} \end{equation} This gives us two mathematical solutions: w = -1 and w = 3. However, we are looking for a realistic, physical answer. There is no such thing as a negative width of land! Therefore, we discard -1 and select the physically real answer: \begin{equation} w = 3\text{ meters} \tag{4} \end{equation}

The key takeaway here is the nature of the answer. As you advance through your STEM education, you will see much more complicated algebraic equations—higher powers, exponentials, logarithms—but in the end, the solution to an algebraic equation is a number (or a set of numbers).

Hypothesizing the Cooling Curve

Now, let’s check back in on our tea. You should all have your thermometers in your cups. Let’s set up a data table. We will record time, t, in minutes, and temperature, T, in degrees Fahrenheit (^\circF).

Before we take too many data points, I want you to sketch out a hypothesis. If you were to plot the temperature of your tea as a function of time, what would that graph look like?

From our everyday experience—and from the physics of thermodynamics—we know that if we wait long enough, the temperature of the hot water will eventually settle at the temperature of the room. We call this the ambient temperature, denoted as T_a. Our room is air-conditioned and sitting at about T_a \approx 76^\circ\text{F}. It would be crazy if your drink somehow ended up colder than the room!

Because the temperature is always driving toward T_a, it is often much more convenient to track how much hotter the drink is compared to the room, rather than tracking the raw temperature. We call this the temperature deviation, defined as: \begin{equation} \Delta T = T - T_a \tag{5} \end{equation} When you see the capital Greek letter delta (\Delta), it usually means a change or a difference from a reference point. If we plot \Delta T instead of T, we know that if we wait a very long time, the deviation will drop to zero.

If your tea is currently at 150^\circ\text{F} and the room is 70^\circ\text{F}, what is your temperature deviation \Delta T? What will this value be after sitting in the room for three days?

Your current temperature deviation is \Delta T = 150^\circ\text{F} - 70^\circ\text{F} = 80^\circ\text{F}. After three days, the tea will have reached room temperature, meaning the deviation \Delta T will be zero.

So, what is the shape of this curve? As some of you guessed, it should be steep at the start and become less steep over time. Think about drawing a hot bath: initially, it cools down very noticeably, but going from lukewarm to room temperature seems to take forever.

What is a Differential Equation?

This brings us to the core topic of the day. If the solution to an algebraic equation is a single number, what is the solution to a differential equation?

The solution to a differential equation is a function—a curve that you can graph. You are not solving for a single value like "3 meters"; you are solving for an overall behavior, like the cooling curve we just hypothesized.

If I hand you an equation and you solve it to find x = 42, did you just solve an algebraic equation or a differential equation?

You solved an algebraic equation. The solution to an algebraic equation is a specific number or set of numbers. In contrast, the solution to a differential equation is a function that describes a continuous behavior over time or space.

Let’s look at the structure of a basic differential equation. It generally looks something like this: \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dt} \big[ \text{something} \big] = \text{Constant} \times \big[ \text{something} \big] \tag{6} \end{equation}

Let’s break down the notation. The left-hand side, \frac{d}{dt}, is the derivative you have seen in calculus. It represents the time rate of change—how quickly the "something" inside the brackets is changing.

In our experiment, that "something" is the temperature deviation, \Delta T. So, the left side is \frac{d}{dt} \Delta T, which asks: "How fast is the temperature difference dropping right now?"

If we translate Equation 6 into plain English, it says: How fast this "something" changes is proportional to the amount (or size) of that "something" currently present.

Does this match our tea intuition? Yes!

  • When your tea is piping hot (large \Delta T), it cools down very quickly (large time rate of change).

  • When your tea is just barely above room temperature (small \Delta T), it cools down very slowly (small time rate of change).

The Exponential Decay Solution

Let’s write our specific differential equation for the cooling tea. We will use a constant called -r (the negative sign indicates that the temperature is dropping, and r is the rate). \begin{equation} \frac{d}{dt} \Delta T = -r \Delta T \tag{7} \end{equation} This is actually a famous physical law known as Newton’s Law of Cooling.

Even without doing the rigorous calculus to solve this step-by-step, I can tell you right away that the solution—the function that satisfies this rule—is an exponential decay function. It takes the form: \begin{equation} \Delta T(t) = C e^{-rt} \tag{8} \end{equation}

By the way, there are a lot of "T"s in this lecture: t for time, T for temperature, and literal tea! I planned it that way.

Let’s look at the pieces of this solution:

  • \Delta T(t): This is our function. It tells us the temperature deviation at any given time t.

  • e: Euler’s number (approximately 2.718), the base of the natural logarithm.

  • t: Time, which we are measuring in minutes.

  • C: This is a constant that represents our initial condition. Specifically, if you plug in t=0, e^0 = 1, so \Delta T(0) = C. Therefore, C is just our initial temperature deviation, \Delta T_0.

  • r: This is the decay rate (or characteristic decay rate). It dictates how "squished" or "stretched" our cooling curve is.

Let’s calculate C for our classroom. Most of you measured an initial hot water temperature of about 200^\circ\text{F}. Our room temperature is 76^\circ\text{F}. \begin{align} C &= \Delta T(t=0) \tag{9}\\ C &= T(0) - T_a \tag{10}\\ C &= 200^\circ\text{F} - 76^\circ\text{F} = 124^\circ\text{F} \tag{11} \end{align} So, our specific curve starts at 124^\circ\text{F} above room temperature.

Understanding the Decay Rate, r

The only mystery left in our equation is r. I cannot tell you what r is just by looking at the cup; it is an empirical value we have to find from your data. However, we can understand how it behaves.

The basic shape of an exponential decay curve is always the same. The decay rate r just determines how horizontally stretched or compressed that shape is.

  • Large r (Fast Decay): The curve drops sharply. The temperature deviation vanishes quickly.

  • Small r (Slow Decay): The curve is spread out over a long time. The drink stays hot longer.

When I was pouring the water, I tried to give everyone the same amount, but the folks in the back ended up with a bit less water in their cups. This is actually a great accidental variable for our experiment!

Think about it: if you have a tiny splash of hot water, it will cool down to room temperature almost immediately (large r). If I gave you a massive tub of hot water, it would take hours to cool (small r). I am hoping that when we look at the data, we will see a subtle difference in the decay rates between the groups with more water and the groups with less water.

Suppose you pour a tiny espresso and a massive mug of drip coffee at the exact same temperature. Which drink’s cooling curve has a larger decay rate r?

The tiny espresso has a larger decay rate r. Because it has a much smaller volume, it loses its heat to the surrounding room much faster, resulting in a steeper exponential decay curve.

Analyzing Our Experimental Data

Alright, time is up! Please bring your thermometers to the front, dump your cups in the nearest sink, and email me pictures of your data sheets.

I have compiled the data from two different groups into the tables below. Group 1 had a larger volume of water, and Group 2 had a slightly smaller volume. Let’s see if our hypothesis about the cooling curves and the decay rates holds up.

To really understand what this data is telling us, we need to graph it. I have plotted both datasets below, along with a dashed line representing our ambient room temperature (T_a \approx 76^\circ\text{F}).

Look at that! The data beautifully follows the exponential decay curve we derived from our differential equation. Both curves start off dropping rapidly when the temperature deviation is large, and they begin to flatten out as they approach the ambient room temperature.

Furthermore, notice the difference between the two curves. Group 2 (the blue squares) started at a slightly lower temperature, but more importantly, their curve dives downward more aggressively than Group 1’s curve. By minute 20, Group 2 has dropped all the way to 120^\circ\text{F}, while Group 1 is still sitting at 136.3^\circ\text{F}.

This confirms our physical intuition: the smaller volume of water in Group 2’s cup resulted in a larger decay rate r. Their tea lost its heat to the environment much faster.

Next time, we will take this data, plug it into some software, and actually calculate the exact numerical values for r for both groups. But for today, you have successfully seen how a physical phenomenon translates into a differential equation, and how the solution to that equation is a function that perfectly describes the real world. Great job, everyone!
